questions.questionText: What does it mean to synthesize sources?
options: Combine evidence to develop an integrated understanding
Copy each source word for word and preserve its original order
Choose the source with the longest title
Remove every disagreement from the record
questions.correctAnswer: Combine evidence to develop an integrated understanding
questions.explanation: Synthesis connects findings, methods and perspectives across sources to form a coherent understanding.

curriculum.objective: Synthesize diverse evidence by evaluating quality, reconciling disagreement and producing appropriately qualified conclusions.

questions.questionText: Two strong studies disagree. What is the best first analytical response?
options: Average their conclusions without inspection
Compare their methods, samples and contexts
Reject both because disagreement exists
Select the conclusion you preferred beforehand
questions.correctAnswer: Compare their methods, samples and contexts
questions.explanation: Differences in design, population or setting may explain disagreement and help define where each result applies.

curriculum.objective: Synthesize diverse evidence by evaluating quality, reconciling disagreement and producing appropriately qualified conclusions.

questions.questionText: Which conclusion is most appropriate when evidence is consistent but comes only from high-income countries?
options: The pattern must apply identically in every country and social context
Geographic scope has no effect on inference
The pattern is supported there, but wider generalization is uncertain
The evidence proves a universal law
questions.correctAnswer: The pattern is supported there, but wider generalization is uncertain
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion should reflect both consistent findings and the geographic limitation of the evidence base.

curriculum.objective: Synthesize diverse evidence by evaluating quality, reconciling disagreement and producing appropriately qualified conclusions.

questions.questionText: A review gives equal weight to a large controlled study and an anonymous unsupported post. What is the main synthesis error?
options: Using more than one source
Acknowledging that sources can differ
Writing a conclusion after reviewing several independent sources
Failing to weight evidence by quality and relevance
questions.correctAnswer: Failing to weight evidence by quality and relevance
questions.explanation: Synthesis should not treat all claims equally; methodological strength, transparency and relevance determine evidential weight.

curriculum.objective: Synthesize diverse evidence by evaluating quality, reconciling disagreement and producing appropriately qualified conclusions.

questions.questionText: What is interdependence?
options: Mutual reliance between connected actors or systems
Complete isolation from outside influence, exchange or consequences
A policy made by one person only
A measurement with no variables
questions.correctAnswer: Mutual reliance between connected actors or systems
questions.explanation: Interdependence means actions and outcomes are linked because actors or systems rely on one another.

curriculum.objective: Analyse global issues as interconnected systems involving feedbacks, trade-offs, power and cross-border effects.

questions.questionText: Why can one country’s carbon emissions affect people elsewhere?
options: National borders permanently block all atmospheric circulation
Greenhouse gases mix globally in the atmosphere
Climate processes occur only locally
Carbon dioxide immediately becomes solid
questions.correctAnswer: Greenhouse gases mix globally in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Atmospheric circulation distributes greenhouse gases, so emissions contribute to global rather than purely national change.

curriculum.objective: Analyse global issues as interconnected systems involving feedbacks, trade-offs, power and cross-border effects.

questions.questionText: A food-export ban protects domestic supply but raises prices in importing countries. What does this illustrate?
options: A decision with no external consequences
The end of all international markets
A policy trade-off transmitted through an interconnected system
A purely cultural issue without material effects
questions.correctAnswer: A policy trade-off transmitted through an interconnected system
questions.explanation: National action can improve one goal locally while shifting costs through trade networks to other populations.

curriculum.objective: Analyse global issues as interconnected systems involving feedbacks, trade-offs, power and cross-border effects.

questions.questionText: Which intervention best addresses antibiotic resistance as a global system problem?
options: Treat resistance as one hospital’s private issue
Increase unnecessary prescribing everywhere
Stop sharing outbreak and laboratory data
Coordinate stewardship, surveillance and access across countries
questions.correctAnswer: Coordinate stewardship, surveillance and access across countries
questions.explanation: Resistance crosses borders and sectors, requiring coordinated use, monitoring, infection control and equitable treatment access.

curriculum.objective: Analyse global issues as interconnected systems involving feedbacks, trade-offs, power and cross-border effects.

questions.questionText: Which ethical principle focuses on fair distribution of benefits and burdens?
options: Justice
Popularity
Tradition alone
Technical speed
questions.correctAnswer: Justice
questions.explanation: Justice concerns fairness in how benefits, risks, opportunities and burdens are distributed.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate policy options using rights, consequences, justice, feasibility, stakeholder power and uncertainty.

questions.questionText: A health policy produces large overall benefits but places most costs on a vulnerable minority. What tension is central?
options: File size versus internet speed
Aggregate benefit versus distributive justice
Weather forecasting versus map scale
Grammar versus visual design
questions.correctAnswer: Aggregate benefit versus distributive justice
questions.explanation: The policy may maximize total benefit while distributing burdens unfairly, creating a consequential and justice-based conflict.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate policy options using rights, consequences, justice, feasibility, stakeholder power and uncertainty.

questions.questionText: Why should policy evaluation include feasibility as well as desirability?
options: Desirable policies never require implementation
Feasibility measures only public popularity
A preferred option may lack resources, capacity or compliance
Ethics is unrelated to real-world effects
questions.correctAnswer: A preferred option may lack resources, capacity or compliance
questions.explanation: An option cannot achieve intended outcomes if institutions, budgets, technology or public cooperation are insufficient.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate policy options using rights, consequences, justice, feasibility, stakeholder power and uncertainty.

questions.questionText: A government tests facial recognition in public spaces without notice or appeal. Which safeguard most directly improves procedural fairness?
options: Secret criteria controlled by the vendor
Permanent retention of every captured image
Removal of accuracy and bias audits
Transparent rules, independent oversight and challenge rights
questions.correctAnswer: Transparent rules, independent oversight and challenge rights
questions.explanation: Procedural fairness requires understandable rules, accountable review and a meaningful way to contest decisions.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate policy options using rights, consequences, justice, feasibility, stakeholder power and uncertainty.

questions.questionText: What does reliability mean in research?
options: A method gives consistent results when repeated
A result supports the researcher’s preference
Every participant gives the same opinion
The study uses only qualitative evidence
questions.correctAnswer: A method gives consistent results when repeated
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns consistency of measurement or procedure across repetitions, observers or items.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate research validity, reliability, causality, ethics and uncertainty using design and statistical reasoning.

questions.questionText: Why does random assignment strengthen a controlled experiment?
options: It guarantees a very large sample
It helps balance confounding factors between groups
It removes the need for an outcome measure
It ensures participants know their group
questions.correctAnswer: It helps balance confounding factors between groups
questions.explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic group differences, making the treatment a more plausible cause of outcome differences.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate research validity, reliability, causality, ethics and uncertainty using design and statistical reasoning.

questions.questionText: A study finds a statistically significant effect with a very small effect size. What is the best interpretation?
options: The effect must be large in real life
Statistical significance proves perfect measurement
The effect may be real but have limited practical importance
The null hypothesis becomes impossible forever
questions.correctAnswer: The effect may be real but have limited practical importance
questions.explanation: Statistical significance addresses evidence against chance under a model, while effect size addresses magnitude and practical relevance.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate research validity, reliability, causality, ethics and uncertainty using design and statistical reasoning.

questions.questionText: Researchers stop collecting data as soon as p falls below 0.05 without a pre-set rule. What risk increases?
options: Perfect replication across future samples
Elimination of sampling variability
Automatic correction of measurement bias
A false-positive result from optional stopping
questions.correctAnswer: A false-positive result from optional stopping
questions.explanation: Repeatedly checking and stopping at significance inflates the chance of finding a seemingly significant result by chance.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate research validity, reliability, causality, ethics and uncertainty using design and statistical reasoning.

questions.questionText: Why should communication be adapted for its audience?
options: Different audiences need appropriate context and language
Evidence changes truth for each audience
Technical terms are always clearer
One format is equally accessible to everyone
questions.correctAnswer: Different audiences need appropriate context and language
questions.explanation: Audience knowledge, needs and access shape which explanations, formats and detail levels communicate accurately.

curriculum.objective: Communicate complex conclusions for audiences and critically reflect on limitations, positionality and future improvement.

questions.questionText: Which visual choice best communicates uncertainty in a numerical estimate?
options: Display only a precise number with no context
Show an interval or range around the estimate
Remove labels from the axes
Use decorative icons instead of values
questions.correctAnswer: Show an interval or range around the estimate
questions.explanation: An interval makes the plausible range visible and avoids presenting an estimate as exact.

curriculum.objective: Communicate complex conclusions for audiences and critically reflect on limitations, positionality and future improvement.

questions.questionText: What is positionality in reflective research?
options: The geographic coordinates of every participant
A rule that prevents any interpretation
How a researcher’s identity and context may shape the work
The order of slides in a presentation
questions.correctAnswer: How a researcher’s identity and context may shape the work
questions.explanation: Positionality examines how the researcher’s background, relationships and assumptions can influence questions and interpretation.

curriculum.objective: Communicate complex conclusions for audiences and critically reflect on limitations, positionality and future improvement.

questions.questionText: A presentation gives a strong recommendation but hides major evidence gaps. Which revision is most responsible?
options: Delete all references to limitations
Express greater certainty than the data supports
Replace analysis with emotional slogans
State the gaps and qualify the recommendation accordingly
questions.correctAnswer: State the gaps and qualify the recommendation accordingly
questions.explanation: Responsible communication makes uncertainty and limitations visible so audiences can judge the recommendation proportionately.

curriculum.objective: Communicate complex conclusions for audiences and critically reflect on limitations, positionality and future improvement.
